entry.title: Inside Argo CD’s Source: How the GitOps Controller Turns Git Commits into Cluster State

link.title: Inside Argo CD’s Source: How the GitOps Controller Turns Git Commits into Cluster State

entry.content:
GitOps is the operating model where Git is the source of truth for what runs in your cluster, and a controller’s only job is to close the loop between the repository and the API server. For AI/ML infrastructure this matters more than almost anywhere else. Model serving stacks are stacks of YAML: a Kubernetes Deployment for the inference server, a Service and Ingress in front of it, and a PVC or object-store credential Secret behind it. When a new model checkpoint passes evaluation, the “promotion” step should not be a human typing kubectl apply at 2 a.m. — it should be a commit to a Git repo that a machine reconciles faithfully.

Argo CD is the most widely deployed implementation of that idea. It is a Kubernetes controller written in Go (CNCF graduated, packaged with Helm charts), and it watches custom resources called Applications. Each Application declares two halves: a source (a Git repo, revision and path) and a destination (a cluster and namespace). Argo CD continuously renders the manifests from Git, diffs them against what actually exists in the destination cluster, and reports or corrects the drift. The same contract works for a five-file demo and for a fleet-wide model rollout, which is why ML platform teams adopt it for promotion between staging and production.

This post is a source tour of the three main components — the application controller, the repo-server render service, and the API server — based on the code at master (fresh sparse checkout). Two architecture diagrams generated from the source tree anchor the discussion; every file path and symbol below was grepped and line-checked against that checkout.

Overview: the API server fronts users, the repo-server renders Git into manifests, and the application controller diffs and syncs them into target clusters, sharing a Redis cache and a Kubernetes-backed configuration store.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Git repository — the declarative source of truth. Nothing in Argo CD mutates Git; it only reads it, which is why commits are the promotion unit for model rollouts.
  • Repo server — a stateless gRPC render service, started by NewServer, L49. It clones repositories, checks out revisions and turns Helm charts, Kustomize overlays or raw YAML into a flat list of manifests.
  • API server — the gateway for the UI, CLI and CI systems, assembled in NewServer, L331. It handles auth, RBAC and Application CRUD, and serves a watch stream via Watch, L1266.
  • Application controller — the reconciliation brain, started by Run, L930 with separate worker pools for status refreshes, operations and hydration.
  • App state manager — the comparison half, CompareAppState, L682, which produces the diff between rendered target state and live objects.
  • Sync engine — the acting half, SyncAppState, L160, which applies, prunes and waits across sync waves.
  • Shared infrastructure — the Redis-backed cache in NewCache, L46 and the configuration store NewDB, L134, which persists clusters and repo credentials as Kubernetes Secrets.
  • Target clusters — where the work lands; every managed object gets tracking applied by SetAppInstanceLabel, L23 so Argo CD knows which Application owns it.

Detail view: the refresh queue feeds CompareAppState, the operation queue feeds SyncAppState, and both lean on the repo-server, the cluster store and the shared caches.

The Reconciliation Loop

The controller’s main loop lives in controller/appcontroller.go. Run, L930 starts three worker pools: status processors drain the refresh queue, operation processors drain the operation queue, and hydration processors handle the source-hydrator flow. Each status worker runs processAppRefreshQueueItem, L2125: it pops an Application from the queue, checks project locks, then asks the app state manager to compare.

Comparison is the heart of the loop. CompareAppState, L682 first calls GetRepoObjs, L229 to fetch rendered manifests from the repo-server, then NormalizeTargetObjects, L574 stamps tracking identity and strips noise so diffs stay clean. Live state comes from informer caches per cluster, and the result carries both sync status and health. Health itself is aggregated by setApplicationHealth, L25, which honors per-resource Lua overrides. Each successful comparison is recorded by persistRevisionHistory, L1268, which is what makes later rollbacks possible.

If the application’s sync policy is automated and status is OutOfSync, the refresh path calls autoSync, L2830 to create a sync operation — that is the self-healing behavior that reverts a manual kubectl edit minutes after it happens. Operations are consumed by processAppOperationQueueItem, L1057, which delegates to the sync engine. Separately, Run, L56 keeps the cluster cache fresh with API counts so the UI can show cluster load.

Rendering Manifests in the Repo Server

The repo-server is deliberately stateless so it scales horizontally. GenerateManifest, L667 is the entry RPC the controller and API server call. On a cache miss it proceeds to runManifestGen, L847, which needs an actual working tree: checkoutRevision, L3131 pins the exact commit, including submodules, before any template engine runs.

The underlying Git plumbing is in util/git/client.go. Fetch, L720 retrieves objects with retry, and Checkout, L814 resolves the revision and updates the working copy. Because rendering depends on Helm and Kustomize binaries, the repo-server image bundles those tools; the manifest cache lives in the shared Redis tier so multiple replicas answer consistently. For UI parameter editing, GetAppDetails, L2555 exposes Helm values and Kustomize images without a full render.

The Sync Engine, Waves and Hooks

Syncing is not one apply. SyncAppState, L160 groups resources into sync waves and phases (PreSync, Sync, PostSync), waits between waves, and honors maintenance windows through syncWindowPreventsSync, L730. Hooks — Jobs that must complete before traffic shifts, like an eval harness validating a model before it serves — are orchestrated in the same state machine. Per-resource outcomes are seeded by newSyncOperationResult, L137 and written back into the Application’s operationState, so progress is visible in real time in the UI.

For an ML platform this phasing is exactly what a canary model promotion needs: PreSync runs the dataset validation job, the wave containing the new Deployment applies, and PostSync flips the Helm values or traffic weights only after the readiness gates pass.

The API Server Surface

Everything users touch flows through server/server.go. NewServer, L331 wires the service set, RBAC enforcer, OIDC/Dex session management and settings watchers, then Run, L598 serves a gRPC listener and an HTTP gateway built by newHTTPServer, L1247 for gRPC-Web, Swagger and health endpoints. The application package implements the gRPC surface: Get, L792 reads from informer caches rather than hitting etcd directly, and Sync, L2120 validates RBAC and sync options, resolves source revisions, then writes the operation onto the Application resource — the controller picks it up from its watch, so API server and controller never call each other directly. Cluster and repository credentials live behind ListClusters, L73 in the Secret-backed store, keeping etcd as the only database.

From Install to Your First Model

Getting from zero to a synced Application takes three steps. First, install: apply the Argo CD manifests (kubectl create namespace argocd, then kubectl apply -n argocd -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/stable/manifests/install.yaml), or install through the official Helm chart. You get the three components from this tour, a Redis instance, and a repo-server with Helm/Kustomize available inside. For a cluster already running containerd-based Kubernetes nodes, no special host setup is required — Argo CD is a normal set of controller pods.

Second, connect a repository. Push your model-serving manifests (the inference Deployment, Service, and a ConfigMap with model version) into a Git repo, then either register it in the UI/CLI (argocd repo add) or rely on credentials stored in the Secret-backed config store.

Third, create and sync an Application:

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: llm-serving
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://git.example.com/ml/platform.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: overlays/prod
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: serving
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: false
      selfHeal: true

Apply that with kubectl, and the controller reconciles it: the repo-server renders overlays/prod, CompareAppState diffs against live state, and with automated enabled the sync engine applies the result. Promoting a new model version becomes a Git commit; the controller does the rest, and selfHeal reverts any out-of-band cluster changes.

Honest Limits

Everything above comes from the source and README of the current master tree — no benchmarks were invented here. A few caveats. The diagrams are hand-authored simplifications built from the file tree; they show component relationships, not every call path. The source tour reflects master at the time of writing, and this codebase moves fast — line numbers cited (like GenerateManifest, L667) will shift as the code evolves, though the symbol names are stable. ApplicationSets and the notification controller live in the repository but outside the four directories examined here, so they are not covered. Performance characteristics — render latency, reconciliation throughput, cache hit rates — depend on repository size, cluster count and resource volume; nothing here is a benchmark. Finally, GitOps removes manual drift, not misconfigurations: a bad commit syncs just as faithfully as a good one, so review gates and sync windows still matter.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of Argo CD showing how the application controller, repo-server render service and API server cooperate to sync Git into Kubernetes clusters.

entry.title: containerd Source Tour: The Daemon, the Shim Protocol, and the Snapshot Layer

link.title: containerd Source Tour: The Daemon, the Shim Protocol, and the Snapshot Layer

entry.content:
Every AI inference service you deploy — a Triton server, a vLLM worker, or a plain FastAPI wrapper around a fine-tuned model — exists as a container on some Linux host. On most modern clusters, and on plenty of single-box GPU servers, the process that actually creates those containers is not a heavyweight suite but containerd: an industry-standard container runtime daemon whose job, in the words of its own README, is to manage the complete container lifecycle of its host, covering image transfer and storage, container execution and supervision, and the low-level storage behind all of it.

Because it sits one layer below the orchestrators that ML teams touch daily, containerd quietly decides how fast a model image lands on disk, how a crash inside a model server gets observed, and how a root filesystem is assembled from OCI layers. This post is a source tour of the containerd/containerd repository on its main branch: the plugin-registered gRPC services, the runtime v2 shim protocol, and the snapshot storage layer. Two architecture diagrams anchor the walk, and every claim below links to a concrete file and line so you can verify each step in your own editor.

Why should an ML engineer read a container runtime? Because every cold start of an inference pod is a story about containerd internals: a registry resolver fetching blobs, an unpacker applying layers into a snapshotter, a shim process supervising your GPU server, and an event bus reporting what happened upstream. Once you can read that story, scaling AI workloads stops being folklore.

The containerd daemon in one page: clients hit gRPC services, services delegate to core managers, managers spawn per-container shims, and storage lives behind the bolt metadata database.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The daemon entrypoint main, L260 builds a server in a goroutine and then calls srv.Start(ctx), serving until the process is signaled.
  • Server.New, L125 does not hand-wire anything; LoadPlugins, L313 walks the plugin registry that each package filled at init() time.
  • Each service is one such plugin: the task service registers itself with ID "tasks" at registry.Register, L36 and mounts itself as the public tasks API in Register, L57.
  • Task RPCs flow into NewTaskManager, L138, which routes by namespace and container ID to the right shim connection.
  • Shims are owned by NewShimManager, L157; its Start, L205 launches one shim process per container.
  • On the storage side, the Snapshotter interface, L281 is the contract every filesystem driver implements, and NewDB, L120 creates the single bolt database under everything.
  • Image work enters through NewResolver, L158 and lands via NewUnpacker, L180.

The detailed view: the image path from resolver to unpacker, the task path from ctr to the runc shim over ttrpc, and the snapshot path from Prepare down to bolt metadata.

The Plugin System: Everything Is a Service

The daemon core is small on purpose. Server.New builds an InitContext per plugin, and LoadPlugins instantiates registered plugins in dependency order. You can see that contract concretely in the snapshots service: its InitFn declares that it Requires the metadata plugin, and only then returns m.(*metadata.DB).Snapshotters() at Snapshotters, L40 — one snapshotter instance per configured storage driver name.

Every gRPC service you know from ctr is such a plugin. The task service we saw above; content follows the same shape, registering with ID "content" at ID, L31 and adapting the internal store into the public API with New, L55. Images and containers register identically — ID "images" at ID, L34 and ID "containers" at ID, L35. The practical effect is that you can build a custom containerd binary that adds or swaps services without touching the daemon core, which is exactly how the CRI integration ships as a plugin.

Two plugins deserve special attention for the rest of the story. The transfer service registers with ID "transfer" at ID, L49 and exposes the streaming image-transfer API; internally, NewTransferService, L51 wires a content store, an image store, and a transfer configuration into the engine that orchestrates a pull from resolver fetch to snapshotter commit. The events service, meanwhile, binds the in-process exchange in NewService, L66 — it is the daemon’s nervous system, and we will meet it again when a shim announces that a container has exited.

Runtime v2: Tasks, Shims, and the ttrpc Hop

When a task RPC arrives, the local tasks backend constructed in initFunc, L102 hands it to the runtime v2 machinery. The ShimManager.Start path first creates the on-disk bundle with NewBundle, L50, then execs the shim binary in binary.Start, L66, which parses the bootstrap address the shim prints on stdout and dials it.

The shim itself is a separate Go binary: cmd/containerd-shim-runc-v2. Its main, L30 calls shim.RunShim with manager.NewShimManager("io.containerd.runc.v2"), and the in-shim task service built by NewTaskService, L63 registers on a ttrpc server at RegisterTTRPC, L289. The wire contract is the protobuf definition at shim.proto — CreateTask, Start, Kill, Shutdown, plus streaming IO. On the daemon side, ttrpcV2Bridge, L89 adapts those shim RPCs to the daemon’s task API, chosen by NewTaskClient, L65. Once connected, the shim handle is wrapped in a task object whose Create, L713 forwards the OCI spec and the rootfs mounts the snapshotter produced, and whose Start, L807 actually begins the user process inside the bundle.

Why one process per container? Three reasons visible in the code. First, crash isolation: a dead shim is detected and cleaned up in cleanupAfterDeadShim, L146 without taking the daemon down. Second, daemon restart survival: on startup, loadShim, L80 reconnects to live shims from disk state. Third, events: the shim publishes task exits through the exchange’s Publish, L80, and the events service mirrors that to external subscribers via its own RegisterTTRPC, L80.

The Snapshot Layer: How Root Filesystems Get Built

Every layer of every image eventually becomes a snapshot. The Snapshotter interface is deliberately tiny: Prepare, L325 creates an active snapshot and returns mounts — the same Mount struct, L35 the runtime later applies — while Commit, L350 seals changes into a committed snapshot that other snapshots can descend from. The file’s own comments walk through this prepare-mount-commit lifecycle, and it is worth reading as a design doc.

Bookkeeping lives in the bolt metastore: CreateSnapshot, L217 persists keys and parent chains, and GetSnapshot, L182 reconstructs the parent chain for mount time. All of this hangs off the one metadata database from NewDB, which also stores containers, images, namespaces, and leases — that is why the snapshots service can only initialize after the metadata plugin. Alongside Prepare, the interface offers View, whose doc comments describe it as behaving identically except that the mounts may not be writable and Commit is forbidden — the read-only path used when many containers share one image’s root filesystem without copying it.

The content store underneath is equally contractual: the Store interface, L41 composes a Provider, L56 for reading blobs by digest from an Ingester, L64 for writing them. Because blobs are addressed by content hash, two images that share layers share storage automatically — the deduplication is a property of the addressing scheme, not an extra feature.

The unpacker is where image work meets storage. NewUnpacker wraps a handler whose Unpack, L205 fetches layers, applies them, and commits snapshots — with explicit locking per chain ID and snapshotter at lockSnChainID, L836 so that concurrent pulls of the same base image do not redo each other’s work.

From Install to Your First Model

Building the daemon from source is refreshingly ordinary. Per BUILDING.md, you need a Go compiler covering one of the two most recent major versions, then:

git clone https://github.com/containerd/containerd
cd containerd
make
sudo make install

The make and sudo make install steps are exactly what the document prescribes, and runc must already be installed because, as that document states, it is the default runtime required to run containerd. With containerd on your PATH, start the daemon in one terminal; it will log containerd successfully booted and begin serving its socket. In another terminal, use the ctr client — described in its own help text as an unsupported debug and administrative client at ctr main, L87, which is fine for learning:

sudo ctr images pull docker.io/tritonserver:latest
sudo ctr run --rm -t docker.io/tritonserver:latest demo

Watch the pieces from this post fire in sequence: the transfer service resolves the reference, the docker resolver ingests blobs into the content store, the unpacker commits snapshots, and a shim starts under the daemon. ctr events will stream the topic notifications as they happen. When you outgrow single-box serving, the same daemon becomes the kubelet’s runtime through the CRI plugin, and Kubernetes scheduling decisions start flowing through the shim hop we traced above — our Kubernetes tour covers that side of the boundary.

Honest Limits

Sticking to what the source and docs actually claim: containerd is a daemon for Linux and Windows per the README’s opening line, but on macOS you need a third-party runtime to run containers at all, per BUILDING.md. The btrfs snapshotter requires the btrfs kernel module and tools on Linux, and checkpoint/restore features require criu — both stated in the README’s runtime requirements. runc is mandatory, not optional. The ctr client is explicitly unsupported for anything beyond debugging and administration; production environments interact through higher-level clients such as the CRI plugin. And to be clear about scope: this post makes no performance or benchmark claims — the only timing number in the daemon’s output is an informational boot log. Finally, main is a moving target; the line numbers here were verified against the tree at writing time, and PRs may shift them.

Where This Fits in Your Stack

The pattern here — thin API services over a versioned metadata store, supervision delegated to per-unit processes over a small RPC protocol, storage behind one narrow interface — shows up across the infrastructure you already run for ML. etcd makes the same trade in the coordination world, as our etcd source tour shows; Prometheus strips its ingest down to append-only blocks much like content-addressed blob stores, which we walked in the Prometheus post; and if your containers serve models, the Triton deep dive is the natural next read. containerd is the quiet layer under all of them — worth knowing line by line.
entry.summary: A line-linked walk through the containerd Go source, from plugin-registered gRPC services to the runc shim protocol and the snapshot storage layer that assembles every container root filesystem.

entry.title: CRI-O Source Tour: How Kubernetes’ Leanest Runtime Speaks CRI in Go

link.title: CRI-O Source Tour: How Kubernetes’ Leanest Runtime Speaks CRI in Go

entry.content:
When you schedule a large language model pod onto a Kubernetes node, someone has to actually fork the container process, mount the model weights, wire the network namespace, and keep the thing supervised after the scheduler moves on. On many clusters that someone is CRI-O: a lean, OCI-native container runtime whose entire job is to implement the Kubernetes Container Runtime Interface (CRI) and stop there. Its own CLI usage string in cmd/crio/main.go says it plainly — the scope of crio is tied to the scope of the CRI — which is exactly why inference nodes like it. No Docker API compatibility layer, no embedded build system, no plugin bazaar; just the RPC surface the kubelet needs.

That minimalism matters for AI infrastructure. A GPU box running LLM inference wants its control plane small and predictable, because the interesting resource contention — KV cache, device memory, page cache for weights — is already fierce. CRI-O delegates image handling to the containers/image and containers/storage stacks (the same lineage as Podman), delegates process supervision to conmon plus an OCI runtime like runc, and can route VM-shaped pods to Kata Containers or gVisor through the containerd shim v2 protocol. If you have read our containerd tour, think of CRI-O as the sibling that chose integration-by-subtraction: instead of hosting runtimes behind gRPC shims by default, it talks to runc directly through conmon and only reaches for shims when a sandbox asks for one.

This post is a source tour of the cri-o/cri-o repository on its main branch. We generated two interactive architecture diagrams directly from the Go sources — an overview and a detail view — and every file path, symbol and line number below was verified against the tree at read time. We also have earlier tours of kubernetes and moby if you want the scheduler side and the Docker lineage side of this story.

Overview: one Server struct implements both CRI services; a lib.ContainerServer owns state and hands out the storage layer; oci.Runtime dispatches to a conmon-based or shim-v2 implementation per runtime handler.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Server, L69 — a single Go struct implements both the RuntimeService and ImageService CRI APIs; the comment above the type declaration says exactly that, which explains why every RPC lives as a method file in server/.
  • New, L436 — the wiring constructor: lib.New for shared state, a hostport manager, the streaming server, NRI hooks and an OCI artifact store, all assembled before the gRPC socket accepts traffic.
  • ContainerServer, L48 — the state core: sandbox and container stores plus ID indexes. Its StorageRuntimeServer (L164) and StorageImageServer (L140) accessors are how RPC methods reach the storage layer.
  • RunPodSandbox, L69 — the pod-level entrypoint; the Linux implementation in runPodSandbox, L471 orchestrates sandbox storage, namespaces, network setup and the pause-image infra container.
  • CreateContainer, L429 — the heaviest RPC in the tree: OCI spec generation, volume and secret mounts, user mapping, devices and seccomp before anything is persisted.
  • PullImage, L32 — collapses concurrent pulls of the same reference through a pullOperationsInProgress map (declared at server.go, L85), so a pod storm does not download the same model layer ten times.
  • Runtime, L47 — a map of runtime handler name to a RuntimeImpl interface (L60); dispatch happens in RuntimeImpl() at L321, keyed by the handler each pod requests.
  • CreateContainer, L120 — the conmon-plus-runc implementation for ordinary pods; its twin at runtime_vm.go, L167 speaks shim v2 for Kata and gVisor sandboxes.

Detail: per-RPC flow through server methods, the storage runtimeService that turns images into snapshots, and the two runtime implementations behind the dispatch layer.

Two Runtimes Behind One Interface

The cleanest design decision in CRI-O is the RuntimeImpl interface in internal/oci/oci.go. Every lifecycle verb — Create, Start, Stop, Delete, Exec, Attach, PortForward, even Checkpoint — is defined once as a Go interface, and the Runtime struct keeps one implementation per configured runtime handler. ValidateRuntimeHandler (oci.go, L119) rejects requests naming a handler that is not in the config, and the handler selection itself comes straight from each RunPodSandbox request.

The default implementation is runtimeOCI, documented at runtime_oci.go, L71 as the implementation “relying on conmon” — a small, crash-resilient supervisor that execs the OCI runtime, daemonizes the container, and reports the PID back through a file that ReadConmonPidFile (L1696) later consumes. The alternative, runtimeVM, spawns a containerd-compatible shim v2 daemon in startRuntimeDaemon (runtime_vm.go, L331) and parses the ttrpc address from the shim’s stdout in ParseShimAddress (L305) — modern shims answer with JSON bootstrap parameters, legacy ones with a raw address. One interface, two very different process topologies, zero conditional soup in the server code.

Images, Snapshots and the Storage Layer

CRI-O’s storage story is a thin, opinionated wrapper over containers/storage and containers/image. On the image side, imageService.PullImage (internal/storage/image.go, L958) resolves the reference, enforces signature policy, and copies layers into the local store; UntagImage (L1101) and DeleteImage (L1135) close the loop behind RemoveImage (server/image_remove.go, L17).

The read side of the image API is just as direct. ListImages (server/image_list.go, L15) walks the store and reuses buildImageResult from the storage service, and ImageStatus (server/image_status.go, L22) resolves whatever the kubelet sends — a full digest, a tag, or a short prefix — through CandidatesForPotentiallyShortImageName (internal/storage/image.go, L1176) before giving up. That tolerance for loose references is deliberate: the kubelet, the pod spec, and crictl all speak slightly different dialects of “this image”.

On the container side there is an elegant reuse: runtimeService.CreatePodSandbox (internal/storage/runtime.go, L358) and runtimeService.CreateContainer (L443) both funnel into createContainerOrPodSandbox (L179). A pod sandbox is, from the storage perspective, just a container created from the pause image — the infra container that holds the network and IPC namespaces every workload joins. The same helper stamps SELinux mount labels and records the container metadata the rest of the daemon reads back in StartContainer (L570) and StopContainer (L597). For a node pulling multi-gigabyte model weights, this layer is also where the dedupe in PullImage pays off: identical layers across inference pods exist once on disk.

From Install to Your First Model

Building CRI-O from source is a standard Go-plus-tools flow. Clone the repository, then run make bin/crio — the target is declared in the Makefile at L212 and compiles cmd/crio into bin/. A full local install, including man pages, shell completions, systemd units and the default configuration, is one more command: make install, defined at Makefile, L255.

Next, emit the effective configuration with crio config — the ConfigCommand that main() registers in cmd/crio/main.go, L205 — and review it; the daemon revalidates everything through Config.Validate (pkg/config/config.go, L1276) at startup anyway. Then point the kubelet at CRI-O with --container-runtime-endpoint=unix:///run/crio/crio.sock; that socket is opened by server.Listen in cmd/crio/main.go, L369 from the configured listen path, and both CRI services are registered on it at L462–463.

For a smoke test without a full cluster, crictl works against the same socket: crictl --runtime-endpoint unix:///run/crio/crio.sock pull <image> then runp and run. And for your first model: install CRI-O on every GPU node, join them to a cluster the usual way (kubeadm takes the runtime endpoint per node), then schedule an inference server pod that requests GPUs through the standard Kubernetes device-plugin mechanism. From the kubelet’s point of view nothing changes from our kubernetes tour — the CRI boundary absorbs the runtime swap.

Lifecycle Details Worth Knowing on GPU Nodes

Three implementation details matter when you run long-lived inference pods. First, sandbox teardown is deliberately idempotent: StopPodSandbox (server/sandbox_stop.go, L16) returns an empty, successful response when the pod is already gone, matching CRI’s expectation, and the Linux path stops every workload container before tearing down the network and infra container. Second, CRI-O carries a hooks framework — HooksRetriever is defined at runtime_handler_hooks.go, L38 — with dedicated high-performance hooks (cpu-load-balancing, IRQ affinity) that CPU-pinned low-latency pods trigger via runtime handlers. Third, checkpoint/restore is a first-class path: StartContainer (server/container_start.go, L18) detects when CreateContainer was handed a checkpoint archive and jumps into ContainerRestore (L43) instead of a cold start — handy for migrating pods that have already paid a long model-load penalty.

The interactive paths get the same treatment. ExecSync (server/container_execsync.go, L15) funnels a command into ExecSyncContainer (internal/oci/runtime_oci.go, L611) and blocks until conmon reports an exit code, while the streaming variants attach to a long-running conmon server instead of re-execing. For interactivity CRI-O keeps a per-container conmon server object modeled by runtimePod (internal/oci/runtime_pod.go, L30), which is how exec, attach and port-forward sessions survive daemon restarts without leaking processes. If you have ever wondered why kubectl exec into a pod keeps working right after the runtime daemon upgrades, this split between the CRI front end and the per-container supervisor is the answer.

Honest Limits

Everything above is read from the source tree at the head of main; none of it is a benchmark, and we did not run the daemon for this article. The diagrams are static call-structure maps of verified symbols — they show which functions reference which, not runtime latency or memory cost. “Lean” is CRI-O’s own design claim, grounded in the CRI-only scope statement in its CLI usage text, not a measurement we reproduced. Platform support is broader than people assume but uneven: the tree carries FreeBSD build-tag variants (for example container_create_freebsd.go and server_freebsd.go) alongside Linux-focused files, so treat Linux as the fully featured path. Finally, conmon and the OCI runtimes are separate projects; their internals are out of scope here, and CRI-O trusts their CLI contracts at the boundaries shown in the diagrams.

CRI-O is the runtime you pick when you want Kubernetes to feel like a kernel and nothing else. Between the kubelet’s CRI client, containerd’s shim ecosystem and Docker’s long lineage, the container stack has three great reference implementations — and reading CRI-O’s server/ directory is the fastest way to understand what the CRI contract really demands. If this tour helped, the other runtime deep dives on this blog make good follow-ups; the three together cover every layer a GPU inference node actually runs.
entry.summary: A guided walk through the CRI-O source tree — from the CRI gRPC server down to conmon, runc and shim v2 — with interactive architecture diagrams.

entry.title: Flux from the Source: How the GitOps Toolkit Bootstraps, Syncs and Heals a Cluster

link.title: Flux from the Source: How the GitOps Toolkit Bootstraps, Syncs and Heals a Cluster

entry.content:
Serving a large model in production is an operations problem as much as a modeling problem. A vLLM or Triton inference server is a Deployment, its weights are a PersistentVolume or an object store, its autoscaling is an HPA, and its rollout is YAML. Once “the model service” becomes files in a repository, the fastest way to ship it is to let machines apply those files for you. Flux, whose source we are touring today, is the GitOps toolkit built on exactly that idea: you commit the desired state of a Kubernetes cluster to Git, and controllers inside the cluster pull, reconcile and heal until reality matches the commit. No CI system needs cluster credentials, no engineer runs kubectl at 2 a.m., and every change is reviewed before it exists.

What separates Flux from push-based deployment tools is the direction of the arrow. A webhook-based system asks “what changed upstream?” and pushes to the cluster; Flux’s controllers ask “what does Git say we should be?” on a configurable interval and converge toward that answer, whether the divergence came from a new commit, a manual edit, or a node reboot that wiped a workload. That pull model is also why Flux coexists naturally with the rest of a Kubernetes stack — the controllers are ordinary Deployments, scheduled like any other pod. We have compared Flux with its closest rival, Argo CD, before (see our /argo-cd/ tour); here we stay inside Flux’s own repository and read how the machine is actually put together.

A warning before we start, because honesty matters more than a tidy narrative: the repo we are reading, fluxcd/flux2, is not where the controllers’ core reconcile loops live. It is the home of the flux CLI, the bootstrap machinery, and the install manifests that glue the toolkit together — while the controllers themselves are maintained as sibling repositories and consumed as release artifacts. The diagrams below map what this repo actually contains, with the sibling-repo boundary drawn in.

Overview: the flux CLI bootstraps the toolkit by generating manifests, committing them to Git, applying the controllers, and then watching those controllers pull the same manifests back from Git.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The binary starts at main, L191, which assembles the cobra command tree — one Go file per flux subcommand — and hands off to the command the user typed.
  • bootstrapCmd, L40 is the command that made Flux famous: install the toolkit and wire Git sync in one shot.
  • Run, L98 is the bootstrap orchestrator. It runs five phases in order: reconcile the repository, reconcile the components, reconcile the source secret, write the sync config, then report health.
  • Two implementations satisfy the Reconciler, L56 interface: the GitProviderBootstrapper, L38, which talks to GitHub or GitLab APIs to create the repo and its deploy key, and the plain-Git bootstrapper for everything else.
  • Generate, L40 renders the component manifests from bases bundled into the CLI binary, while GetLatestVersion, L93 resolves which upstream release the images should come from.
  • sync.Generate, L36 writes the two objects that make Flux self-hosting: a GitRepository pointing at the repo you bootstrapped from, and a Kustomization that applies its contents.
  • Apply, L44 is the CLI’s server-side apply. It applies in two stages — CRDs and Namespaces first, everything else second — using a field manager owned by Flux.
  • Finally, NewStatusChecker, L58 polls object conditions with kstatus and Assess, L71 blocks until every component reports Ready.

Detail view: the CLI commands, the bootstrap orchestration, manifest generation, the apply engine, and the seven controller bases that ship as install overlays.

What the flux2 Repo Is — and Is Not

Walk the tree and you find four things. First, cmd/flux: a large but flat collection of command files — install.go defines installCmd, L41, create_kustomization.go defines createKsCmd, L40, build_kustomization.go defines buildKsCmd, L33 — plus an embed file where embeddedManifests, L28 carries bundled install YAML inside the binary. Second, pkg/: the bootstrap engine, manifest generators, status polling, uninstall and plugin support. Third, internal/: the kustomize build engine, flag types, and apply utilities. Fourth, manifests/: kustomize overlays describing every toolkit component.

The fourth item is where the sibling-repo reality shows. The aggregate overlay manifests/install/kustomization.yaml lists seven controller bases — source-controller, kustomize-controller, helm-controller, notification-controller, image-reflector-controller, image-automation-controller and source-watcher — under resources at lines 4 through 12, then pins each image to its ghcr.io/fluxcd/* form at lines 17 through 31. Each base is itself a tiny kustomization that fetches CRDs and a Deployment from the controller’s own GitHub release; for example, manifests/bases/source-controller/kustomization.yaml pulls both artifacts from the fluxcd/source-controller release at lines 4 and 5, and the helm-controller base does the same against fluxcd/helm-controller. So when you run flux install, the binary you downloaded assembles a stack whose brains live in seven other repos. The same is visible in imports: pkg/bootstrap/bootstrap.go at lines 37 through 40 imports Kustomization types from github.com/fluxcd/kustomize-controller/api/v1 and GitRepository types from github.com/fluxcd/source-controller/api/v1. The CLI and the controllers speak the same Kubernetes API, they just do not share a codebase.

Bootstrap: The CLI That Installs Its Own Control Plane

Bootstrap is the most elegant piece of engineering here, because the CLI installs a system whose job is to install itself. bootstrapCmd, L40 validates flags, unpacks the bundled manifests through buildEmbeddedManifestBase, L181 — the bundle itself is produced at release time by manifests/scripts/bundle.sh so the embed compiles — and then calls Run, L98.

The provider flavor, entered via bootstrapGitHubCmd, L39, uses the GitProviderBootstrapper, L38 to create the repository and reconcile a deploy key through ReconcileRepository, L255. The generic path is NewPlainGitProvider, L108, which wraps any Git remote. From there both flows converge on ReconcileComponents, L119: render the component manifests, commit, push, then server-side apply them onto the cluster. ReconcileSyncConfig, L271 commits the sync manifests so the just-installed controllers immediately begin pulling the repo.

The apply step deserves attention. Apply, L44 splits every object into two stages — cluster-scoped definitions like CRDs and Namespaces go first, workloads wait for those to be established — because a Deployment referencing a CRD that does not exist yet is an immediate failure. It then waits on each change-set before proceeding, which is why bootstrap output prints objects in waves. GenerateGit, L67 produces the deploy-key Secret that gives source-controller read access (and, for image automation, write access) to your repository. Every generated artifact funnels through the small Manifest, L30 struct, whose WriteFile materializes it to disk before commit.

Seven Controllers, One Overlay

Once installed, the division of labor follows the source types. The source-controller turns a GitRepository, HelmRepository, OCIRepository or Bucket into a versioned artifact. The kustomize-controller takes a Kustomization, builds it with kustomize, and applies it. The helm-controller does the same for HelmRelease objects, which is how many model-serving charts (vLLM, Triton, anything packaged for /helm/) reach a cluster. The notification-controller closes the loop outward with alerts and receivers, and the two image controllers implement automated image updates: the reflector scans registries for new tags and the automation controller commits version bumps back to Git.

One detail worth pausing on: the CLI contains a second copy of the reconciliation logic for local use. buildKsCmd, L33 renders a Kustomization to stdout without touching the cluster, and it does so through the Builder, L315 engine in internal/build, whose Build, L386 method supports in-memory builds, SOPS secret masking, and remote-source resolution. flux diff kustomization and flux reconcile (defined as reconcileCmd, L42, which annotates live objects to trigger controllers immediately) round out a debugging toolkit that mirrors what the controllers will do — remarkably useful when a rollout misbehaves.

From Install to Your First Model

Here is the shortest honest path from a bare cluster to a Git-synced inference service. Prerequisites: a Kubernetes cluster you administer — any conformant cluster works, ours ran on containerd with images from the /containerd/ ecosystem — plus a Git account and a token.

First, bootstrap. Run flux bootstrap github --owner=your-org --repo=ai-infra --path=clusters/gpu-1 --personal. Internally this is everything from the section above: repo creation, deploy key, component apply, sync config. Within a minute the seven controllers run in the flux-system namespace, and your repository contains a clusters/gpu-1 directory that the cluster now watches.

Second, declare the workload. Clone ai-infra, add apps/base/vllm/deployment.yaml with your model server (vLLM runs as a plain container; mount weights from a PVC or pull them from object storage at startup) and a Service. Then either run flux create kustomization vllm --source=ai-infra --path=./apps/vllm --prune — the createKsCmd, L40 command — or commit the equivalent Kustomization YAML by hand. Commit and push.

Third, watch it converge. Source-controller clones the repo into an artifact, kustomize-controller builds and applies it, and flux get kustomizations shows Ready once the Deployment is healthy. From now on the workflow is: edit YAML, commit, push — done. Scaling from one model to twenty means adding directories, not servers. Rollback is git revert; drift from a manual kubectl edit disappears on the next reconcile because the controllers treat Git, not the API server, as the source of truth.

Honest Limits

Everything in this post comes from reading the flux2 source and manifests on main at the time of writing — no benchmarks were run, and the line numbers will drift as the project moves. The bigger caveat is scope: we toured the CLI, bootstrap machinery and install overlays, but the reconcile loops that do the daily work — how source-controller clones and packages a repo, how kustomize-controller decides what to prune, how helm-controller upgrades a release — live in their sibling repositories and were not read for this post, so any claim about them should go through their own source. Bootstrap also assumes cluster-admin privileges and a reachable Git remote, and its health checks will fail honestly rather than half-install if components never go Ready. Finally, the AI angle here is deployment, not training: Flux keeps inference serving declarative, but it will not schedule a GPU for you, and teams needing heavy multi-tenant isolation on Kubernetes should read the project’s tenant documentation rather than infer it from this tour.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of fluxcd/flux2: the bootstrap CLI, embedded manifests and reconciliation contract that keep AI inference deployments declarative.

entry.title: Helm Source Tour: How the Kubernetes Package Manager Renders Charts and Stores Releases

link.title: Helm Source Tour: How the Kubernetes Package Manager Renders Charts and Stores Releases

entry.content:
Serving an LLM today is rarely one container. A realistic inference stack means a model server such as vLLM or Triton, a GPU device plugin, autoscaling rules, service endpoints, and a pile of config that all have to land in a Kubernetes cluster in the right order. Hand-writing that as raw YAML does not survive contact with version upgrades. Helm is the ecosystem’s answer: it packages an application into a versioned chart, renders the chart’s Go templates into plain Kubernetes manifests, applies them, and remembers what it did so it can roll forward or back. If you run inference workloads on Kubernetes, Helm is the layer between helm install and your pods, and the kubernetes objects you inspect afterward were shaped by this code.

That is why this repository deserves a source tour. Helm is written in Go, the repo layout is unusually clean, and each stage of its life as a tool maps to a package you can read in one sitting: chart loading in pkg/chart, template execution in pkg/engine, install and upgrade orchestration in pkg/action, and release bookkeeping in pkg/storage. Nothing here is hidden behind a control plane; the CLI talks straight to the API server, which also means everything it does is auditable by reading source. The same philosophy we saw in our containerd and cri-o tours — small Go components doing exactly one job — holds here, except Helm’s job is packaging rather than running containers. Charts have become the de facto distribution format for inference stacks: most model-server projects publish one, so knowing what install actually does tells you what will exist in your cluster before the first pod starts.

In this post we walk the main branch of helm/helm from two altitudes. The overview diagram shows the six subsystems and how helm install travels through them. The detail diagram zooms into the functions themselves, each linked to real source lines so you can follow along. By the end you will know where a chart directory becomes a Go struct, where templates become manifests, and where a release revision is stored — spoiler: it is a Secret with a very particular set of labels.

Helm at a glance: the CLI registers install and upgrade actions, every action shares one Configuration, the engine turns chart templates into manifests, and the kube client applies them while release revisions are persisted through the storage layer.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • main is tiny: main, L31 just delegates to the root command, which is where the real CLI tree is assembled in NewRootCmd, L106.
  • Chart content enters through LoadDir, L77 for directories on disk, with archive and file variants alongside it in the same loader package.
  • Everything loads into the Chart, L38 struct, which carries metadata, templates, values, and nested dependencies in memory.
  • Remote references are handled before loading: DownloadTo, L101 fetches an archive once ResolveChartVersion, L365 has mapped a repo name and version to a URL.
  • Rendering is centered on Render, L84, which executes every template and returns a map of manifest strings.
  • The install action Run, L285 orchestrates the whole first install; its twin for upgrades is Upgrade.Run, L164.
  • Both actions share the dependency bag in Configuration, L120: a kube client, a releases storage handle, and cluster capabilities.
  • Releases are recorded through Storage, L53, whose default driver Create, L163 pushes the revision out as a Kubernetes Secret.
  • Actual cluster mutation happens in Client.Build, L555, which parses manifests into a resource list the client can apply.

The detail view traces one install end to end: runInstall loads the chart, the action resolves dependencies and merges values, renderResources drives the engine, the kube client builds and creates resources, and recordRelease persists the revision as a labeled Secret.

Chart Loading: Directory to Struct

A chart on disk is just files: a Chart.yaml, a values.yaml, a templates/ folder. The loader package turns that into typed Go data. LoadDir walks the directory and classifies each file, LoadFile handles a packaged chart file, and LoadArchive at LoadArchive, L160 takes a gzipped tarball straight off the wire. The result is the Chart struct whose metadata — apiVersion, name, version, appVersion — lives in Metadata, L48. Dependencies declared in Chart.yaml are expanded and validated by ProcessDependencies, L32, and the download side is mirrored by the manager in Manager.Update, L157, which refreshes repositories and pulls missing subcharts. The repository definitions themselves are simple entries like Entry, L38 with an index of available chart versions in IndexFile, L82.

One Pass Through the Template Engine

Helm’s engine is a thin, deliberate wrapper over Go’s text/template. The Engine struct at Engine, L39 holds cluster configuration so templates can call lookup against live API state. When rendering starts, allTemplates, L563 recursively collects templates from the parent chart and every subchart, sortTemplates, L536 orders them so underscore-prefixed helpers and partials come first, and initFunMap, L240 registers the function set: include, tpl, toYaml, the lookup function that queries the cluster, plus the Sprig helpers. The whole run happens in render, L301, and errors are re-formatted with file and line context so a broken template points at the offending chart file. There is no incremental compilation and no hidden state between renders; each invocation is a pure function of chart plus values, which is exactly why charts behave the same in CI as on your laptop.

Actions: Install and Upgrade as Two Shapes of the Same Job

All commands delegate to action objects constructed with shared dependencies. NewInstall at NewInstall, L162 returns an Install whose Run method executes a fixed sequence. It first processes dependencies, then merges chart defaults with user values through ToRenderValuesWithSchemaValidation, L36, and then asks the shared renderer renderResources, L279 to produce hooks, a manifest buffer, and release notes — that helper instantiates the engine itself at engine.New, L305. Back in Run, the manifest string is parsed into a typed resource list via Client.Build, resources are created on the API server, and recordRelease, L689 writes the revision.

Upgrade is the more interesting shape. Upgrade.Run, L164 checks the cluster is reachable, then prepareUpgrade, L221 loads the previous revision, optionally re-merges its values through reuseValues, L607, and renders the new manifest. The client then builds two resource lists — the old manifest and the new one — and Client.Update, L808 patches changed resources and deletes removed ones. Lifecycle hooks execute around these steps in execHook, L35, sorted by weight, with delete policies enforced by deleteHookByPolicy, L180.

From Install to Your First Model

Building Helm from source is a two-command affair because the whole product is one Go binary. Clone the repo, then run make build; the target at build, L67 ends up invoking go build against ./cmd/helm as shown at L70, and drops the binary into your bin directory. With that in hand, take any chart directory — for a model-serving experiment, scaffold one whose templates describe a Deployment for your inference server plus a Service — and run helm install gpu-infer ./my-model-chart. Watch the sequence you just read about: the CLI loads the directory, resolves dependencies, renders templates with your values, builds a resource list, and applies it.

Verification is where the storage design becomes visible. Run helm list to see the release, or ask the API server directly with kubectl get secrets -n <namespace> -l owner=helm and you will find one Secret per revision, named after the release and revision number. That works because every stored release carries the labels set by the driver, including owner=helm, name, status, and version. A helm upgrade creates a second Secret rather than mutating the first, which is what makes history and rollback cheap: old revisions are just older rows, never edits.

Releases as Kubernetes Secrets

The storage layer is a facade in Storage, L53 with Create, Update, and History at History, L224, backed by interchangeable drivers. The default is Secrets, L46, whose Create encodes the release and posts a Secret with the release’s identity stamped into labels. The encoder newSecretsObject, L246 sets the object type to helm.sh/release.v1 and labels name, owner (literally the string helm), status, and the revision number. Alternatives ship in the same package: ConfigMaps, L46 for the legacy placement, SQL, L91 for external databases, and an in-memory Memory, L42 for tests. The driver receives a release abstraction rather than a concrete struct, and adapters like releaserToV1Release in the root command bridge the interface to the v1 type at Release, L32, whose embedded Hook, L78 entries record hook weights and delete policies alongside the manifest.

Honest Limits

Everything above was verified by reading the main branch source; no benchmarks or performance claims in this post come from anywhere else. Three caveats for anyone repeating the tour. First, the diagrams compress reality: the kube client does far more than build, create, and update — it also handles deletion, waits, and namespace wiring — and the engine’s function map is richer than the four functions named here. Second, this branch is under active development; we saw interface types such as Releaser threading through storage and CLI code, so exact signatures may move between now and your checkout, though the package layout has been stable for years. Third, our diagrams cover install and upgrade only; rollback, template, and lint re-use the same render core through their own action files, which we did not trace line by line. Finally, Helm only manages what a chart declares — it will happily deploy your model server, but runtime realities like GPU scheduling and pod placement are owned by the layers below it, down through the container runtime to the kernel; see our runc tour for that end of the stack.
entry.summary: A guided walk through the helm/helm Go source showing how charts load, how the template engine renders manifests, and how every release revision ends up as a Kubernetes Secret.

entry.title: Kubernetes From the Source: How kube-apiserver and kubelet Are Wired in Go

link.title: Kubernetes From the Source: How kube-apiserver and kubelet Are Wired in Go

entry.content:
If you serve an LLM in production today, the odds are good that the model runs in a Pod somewhere on a Kubernetes cluster. The scheduler picked a GPU node, the node agent pulled the image, started the container, and reported status back — and every one of those steps was executed by ordinary Go code that you can read on GitHub. Kubernetes is the layer of infrastructure that AI inference sits on, which is exactly why it is worth reading: the guarantees your inference service silently depends on are written in these files.

This post is a source tour of the two binaries at the heart of that arrangement: kube-apiserver, the front door of the control plane, and kubelet, the agent on every node. Rather than describing their behavior from documentation, we walk the actual wiring in kubernetes/kubernetes — the cobra command that boots the server, the chain of API servers it builds, the REST storage where Pod objects live, the watch loop that carries desired state to the node, and the runtime manager that finally talks to containerd. Every symbol below is cited with its file and line on the master branch, so you can click through and see each one in context.

The payoff for AI workloads is concrete. When you wonder why a GPU Pod is stuck in Pending, why a node flips to NotReady under load, or how a probe failure becomes a restart, the answer is always the same small set of functions: something changed in storage, a watch delivered it, a sync loop reconciled reality toward spec. Reading that loop once makes every debugging session afterward feel less like guessing.

The overview: a cobra command builds a chain of API servers, REST storage exposes Pods and other resources, and the kubelet pulls its work through a filtered watch before handing updates to per-pod workers and the CRI runtime.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything starts small: main, L32 is just five lines that construct NewAPIServerCommand, L73 and hand it to a shared CLI runner — all flags, validation and logging live on that command.
  • The command’s RunE, L96 completes the parsed options, validates them, and calls Run, which assembles the actual server.
  • CreateServerChain, L188 builds the delegation chain: the apiextensions server first, then the kube-apiserver itself, then the aggregator that fronts both.
  • The heavy lifting happens in CompletedConfig.New, L318, which installs APIs on the generic server and returns the control-plane Instance.
  • Resource behavior comes from REST storage: the Pod object you kubectl apply is served by the REST struct at storage.go, L74, with validation supplied by the strategy at Strategy, L68.
  • On the node side, NewMainKubelet, L468 assembles the giant Kubelet struct — pod sources, PLEG, runtime, volume and container managers.
  • The wiring between the two halves is NewSourceApiserver, L36, which list-watches only pods whose spec.nodeName equals this node — that one field selector is how work finds its way to the right machine.
  • Startup ends in Run, L1895, which starts status reporting, the volume manager and PLEG before blocking forever in syncLoop, L2693.
  • From there updates flow into podWorkers.UpdatePod, L772, which serializes work per pod UID so each Pod is synced by exactly one goroutine at a time.

The detail view: entrypoint chain and control-plane config on the left, the pod registry and its subresources in the middle, and the kubelet's sources, sync loop, node-lifecycle managers and CRI runtime on the right.

Zoom into the detail view and the story gets more granular. On the left, three entrypoint frames march from main through RunE into the server chain. In the middle, the pod registry fans out into the REST store and its subresources. On the right, the kubelet’s world is grouped by responsibility: wiring (pod sources, pod manager), the sync loop and pod workers, node lifecycle (registration, status, PLEG, volume and container managers), and the CRI runtime that actually creates sandboxes and containers. Tracing any single edge — say podWorkers.UpdatePod down to Kubelet.SyncPod — is a good way to read the code linearly instead of hopping between packages.

Two Binaries, One Conversation

The most important architectural decision in Kubernetes is that the control plane never pushes work to nodes. The kube-apiserver stores objects; the kubelet discovers its work by watching. In pkg/kubelet/config/apiserver.go, NewSourceApiserver creates a reflector over pods with fields.OneTermEqualSelector("spec.nodeName", string(nodeName)) — a server-side filter, so a node only ever receives the handful of Pods it is expected to run. Updates land on a channel produced by config.NewPodConfig, whose mux merges file, HTTP and apiserver sources, and whose storage layer calls basicManager.SetPods on pkg/kubelet/pod/pod_manager.go to refresh the kubelet’s cache of desired and mirror pods.

Durable state, meanwhile, lives behind the API server. When a write succeeds, the object has been committed to the cluster’s store — our etcd source tour covers that component separately. This split is what makes every other component replaceable: the scheduler, controllers and kubelet are all just clients with watches. It also explains the resilience model in AI clusters. If a node loses its network for a minute, nothing is “sent” anywhere; when connectivity returns, the same filtered watch replays the current desired state, and the kubelet converges.

The kubelet answers with status in the opposite direction. registerWithAPIServer at pkg/kubelet/kubelet_node_status.go creates or reuses the Node object, and a jittered syncNodeStatus loop publishes node conditions on a fixed cadence. Pod status takes a different path: the status manager batches per-pod updates and patches them back to the API, which is why kubectl get pod can lag a restart by a few seconds — you are reading a cached, batched report, not the runtime’s live state.

Inside kube-apiserver: Cobra to REST Storage

The server’s boot sequence is a study in layering. main builds one cobra command; RunE turns flags into CompletedOptions; and CreateKubeAPIServerConfig at cmd/kube-apiserver/app/server.go prepares everything — storage factory, admission plugin initializers, service resolver — without running any of it. The comment on that function is refreshingly honest: it “creates all the resources for running the API server, but runs none of them.”

The resulting Instance from pkg/controlplane/instance.go wires the generic server to kube-specific behavior. StorageProviders returns a provider per API group, and each provider hands the mux a set of REST storage objects — one per resource. For Pods, that storage is genericregistry.Store plus a small amount of pod-specific glue: eviction support, and the subresources that make kubectl feel magical. kubectl logs pod/x is served by LogREST in pkg/registry/core/pod/rest/log.go; kubectl exec and kubectl port-forward map to ExecREST and PortForwardREST in rest/subresources.go, which upgrade the HTTP connection into SPDY tunnels to the node. Validation is not an afterthought either: every create and update passes through the strategy’s PrepareForCreate and Validate hooks before the store persists anything, which is why malformed manifests fail at admission with field-level errors instead of surprising the scheduler.

Endpoint reconciliation closes the loop for in-cluster clients. createLeaseReconciler in pkg/controlplane/instance.go keeps the kubernetes service’s endpoints pointed at healthy API servers using Lease objects. Everything above this layer — CRDs, the aggregated APIs that Prometheus adapters and GPU device plugins expose — is just more storage plugged into the same chain, which is why the API surface can grow without changing the boot path.

Inside kubelet: Watch Loop to Container Runtime

syncLoop is deceptively calm: it reads events and hands them to pod workers. The real transaction script is Kubelet.SyncPod at pkg/kubelet/kubelet.go, whose doc comment enumerates the workflow — generate status, admit the pod, create mirror pods for static entries, make directories, wait for volumes, fetch pull secrets, then call the container runtime’s SyncPod. That final call lands in kubeGenericRuntimeManager.SyncPod at pkg/kubelet/kuberuntime/kuberuntime_manager.go, which computes a diff of desired versus actual containers — computePodActions — and then creates sandboxes, pulls images, and starts or kills containers over the CRI gRPC interface.

Around the sync loop live the managers that make a node safe for neighbors. NewContainerManager at pkg/kubelet/cm/container_manager_linux.go sets up cgroups so that Guaranteed pods get their reservation and system daemons stay alive. NewVolumeManager tracks a desired and an actual state of the world for attach and mount operations. And the Pod Lifecycle Event Generator — pleg.NewGenericPLEG at pkg/kubelet/pleg/generic.go — relists runtime state and converts changes into events, which is how a crashed container becomes a sync even when nothing in the API changed. The kubelet also runs its own authenticated HTTP server via ListenAndServeKubeletServer at pkg/kubelet/server/server.go, exposing logs, exec and the metrics that Prometheus scrapes on every node.

From Install to Your First Model

Building from source is a two-command affair. With a working Go toolchain, git clone https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes, cd kubernetes, and run make — the README’s exact quickstart. With Docker instead of a local toolchain, make quick-release performs the same build inside containers and emits release artifacts. Either way you end up with the server binaries, including kube-apiserver and kubelet.

For a real cluster, the practical route is a local tool such as kind or kubeadm rather than hand-rolling the control plane; what matters for this tour is what happens next. Save a minimal Pod manifest:

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: triton-demo
spec:
  containers:
  - name: serve
    image: nvcr.io/nvidia/tritonserver:24.04-py3
    command: ["tritonserver", "--model-repository=/models"]

Then kubectl apply -f pod.yaml. In source terms: the request hits the pod REST storage, passes Strategy.Validate, and is written to storage. Every kubelet’s filtered watch sees it; exactly one node’s selector matches spec.nodeName, so exactly one agent reconciles it — SyncPod pulls the image, starts the sandbox and container, and the status manager reports Running. kubectl logs, kubectl exec and kubectl port-forward all ride the subresources we saw earlier. Swapping the image for a smaller one and adding a Triton model repository config turns the same flow into a genuine inference endpoint. If you need a private image pull, combine this with object storage for artifacts — our MinIO walkthrough fits naturally beside a registry.

Honest Limits

This tour reads only four directories — cmd/kube-apiserver, pkg/kubelet, pkg/registry, pkg/controlplane — so the scheduler, controller-manager and kube-proxy are out of scope, and the generic API machinery largely lives in the staging modules rather than this tree. The build path above is taken verbatim from the README, which also warns that using k8s.io/kubernetes as a Go library is not supported; these internals are free to move between releases, so line numbers here reflect master at the time of writing. Finally, no performance numbers are claimed anywhere in this post — the source defines mechanisms, not benchmarks, and your GPU cluster’s behavior depends far more on your runtime, your workloads and your own configuration choices than on this code. Start from the overview diagram, keep kubectl describe open beside the source, and the whole system reads like the two-binary conversation it is.
entry.summary: A guided source-code tour of Kubernetes showing how the kube-apiserver control plane and the kubelet node agent are wired together in Go.

entry.title: Inside Moby: A Source Tour of the Docker Engine Daemon

link.title: Inside Moby: A Source Tour of the Docker Engine Daemon

entry.content:
Every modern AI workload ships in a container. You pull a CUDA base image, layer on PyTorch or a quantized LLM runtime, and hand it to a scheduler — and the binary quietly doing the heavy lifting behind docker run is dockerd, built from the moby/moby repository. When a training job boots in seconds on a cluster, or a model endpoint scales from zero to fifty replicas, that speed comes from engineering choices made in this Go codebase: layered filesystems, a battle-tested API surface, and an event-driven lifecycle that keeps thousands of containers in check.

The Moby project is the upstream for the Docker Engine. It is not a shim around someone else’s daemon — it is the daemon: an HTTP server, a container state machine, an execution layer, and an image storage system, all in one tree of Go packages. This post is a source tour of the master branch. We will follow a request from the unix socket to the running task, and then look at how the daemon decides between its two storage personalities: the classic graphdriver and the containerd snapshotter that we examined in depth in our ](/containerd/) tour.

The two diagrams below were generated directly from the source tree, so every node links to the exact file and line on GitHub. If you have ever wanted to read the Docker Engine but did not know where to start, this map is for you — and if you run these daemons on a GPU box for inference, the same code paths are what keep your models warm.

Overview of the Docker Engine: the dockerd entrypoint wires listeners and routers into an HTTP server, whose route handlers delegate into the Daemon core; starting a container flows into the execution layer, while image pulls land in the containerd-backed image service with a graphdriver fallback.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The main function in main, L16 is deliberately tiny: it initializes reexec handling and hands off to the command package’s daemon runner.
  • daemonCLI.start, L121 is the real boot sequence — it loads configuration, starts an embedded containerd supervisor when asked, and then binds sockets through loadListeners, L980.
  • The HTTP layer lives in daemon/server, where the Server, L39 type builds its route table in CreateMux, L129. This directory is a recent relocation — the server used to sit in api/server in older releases.
  • A POST /containers/create request lands in postContainersCreate, L553, which decodes the wire payload defined by Config, L25.
  • Start requests funnel from postContainersStart, L283 into ContainerStart, L49 and its workhorse containerStart, L82.
  • The heart of the system is NewDaemon, L874, which validates settings and assembles the sprawling Daemon, L112 struct — stores, services, the network controller, and the containerd client.
  • Each container is tracked by the Container, L73 model, whose lifecycle is guarded by the State, L20 machine.
  • On the right edge, postImagesCreate, L36 streams image pulls into the containerd-backed ImageService, L34, which can fall back to the classic Driver, L92 interface.
  • Underneath it all, the daemon can supervise its own containerd instance: the containerdClient field inside the core struct is a real gRPC client, which is why image and snapshot operations resolve to containerd primitives rather than bespoke code.

The detailed view expands each group: the entrypoint's config and listener setup, every route family the mux serves, the Daemon core's stores and event bus, the execution layer from start request to task, and the storage split between snapshotters and graphdrivers.

Where the overview compresses, the detail view names names: every box is a real type or function in the tree, so the caption doubles as an index for your own reading session. The next three sections walk that diagram group by group.

The Daemon Core

Open daemon/daemon.go and you find the busiest file in the repository. The Daemon struct declares everything the engine owns: a container store, an image service, a network controller, a volume service, a registry client, and the flags usesSnapshotter and containerdClient that tell you which storage generation the daemon booted with. NewDaemon, L874 runs a long checklist before any of that is usable — verifying daemon settings, setting up remapped root, preparing the temporary directory, and resolving runtimes, all within the first sixty lines of the function body.

Container bookkeeping lives one directory down in daemon/container. The NewMemoryStore, L16 constructor returns the in-memory index the daemon consults for every lookup by ID or name, and the root field recorded at L129 points at the data directory where every store and driver ultimately writes. Each entry is a Container struct with an embedded State; the IsRunning, L234 method and the Wait channel at Wait, L165 are what docker wait and restart policies hang off. Broadcasting changes is the job of the pub/sub bus created by New, L26 — the same bus that feeds docker events and the system routes’ streaming handler at getEvents, L293. Configuration itself is validated and merged from flags plus daemon.json by New, L349.

The Execution Layer: From Start Request to Task

The execution layer is where the engine earns its keep. containerStart, L82 coordinates the pieces: it makes sure the container’s state is legal, prepares the root filesystem, asks the networking code to attach the container, and finally sets the state to running through the State machine before handing the request to the runtime integration. The network half is implemented in daemon/container_operations.go, where initializeNetworking, L450 builds a libnetwork sandbox for the container, and network objects themselves are created through CreateNetwork, L296.

Interactive work goes through the exec paths: ContainerExecCreate, L96 registers a pending process against a running container, and ContainerExecStart, L162 attaches streams and launches it — the machinery behind docker exec.

What happens when a process dies? The daemon does not poll. daemon/monitor.go implements ProcessEvent, L193, which reacts to exit events arriving from the containerd task service, updates the state machine, publishes an event, and decides whether a restart policy applies; the exit bookkeeping itself is centralized in handleContainerExit, L35. This event-driven design is the same philosophy that drives the kubelet’s reconciliation loop in Kubernetes, which we compared end to end in our ](/kubernetes/) tour.

Image Storage: Graphdrivers and Snapshotters

Storage is the most interesting migration story in the tree. For years the engine stored images as layer stacks managed by the daemon/graphdriver package — a registry of pluggable backends like overlay2, btrfs, and fuse-overlayfs, each implementing the Driver, L92 interface. That interface composes ProtoDriver and DiffDriver; its Get operation at Get, L53 returns the mountpoint of a layered filesystem and Put releases it.

The modern path instead delegates to containerd’s snapshotter abstraction. The decision is made once at boot by determineImageStoreChoice, L94, and the boolean surfaced by IsGraphDriver, L33 tells the rest of the code which world it is in. The containerd implementation in daemon/containerd/service.go holds a client, a content store, and a map of snapshotter services inside its ImageService, L34 struct. When a container starts, its rootfs view is provided through the reference-counted mounter built by NewMounter, L28, whose Mount, L46 method turns a list of snapshot mounts into a single usable target and safely unmounts it later. Volumes remain a separate concern, exposed to route handlers by VolumesService, L287. For operators, this storage split matters: it is the same snapshotter model we documented in the ](/containerd/) walkthrough, and exporting its metrics pairs naturally with a Prometheus setup like the one in our ](/prometheus/) guide.

From Install to Your First Model

Nothing here requires installing Docker first — you can build the daemon straight from this repository. The steps below were verified against the repository’s own build files.

First, clone and build. The default bake group points at the binary target, declared in docker-bake.hcl, L98 with its output routed to ./bundles/binary at L101:

git clone https://github.com/moby/moby.git
cd moby
make binary

The compilation runs inside BuildKit-driven containers, and the resulting dockerd and docker-proxy binaries are statically linked under ./bundles/binary/. Second, run the freshly built daemon on an isolated socket so it cannot interfere with your system daemon:

sudo ./bundles/binary/dockerd --data-root /tmp/moby-data --exec-root /tmp/moby-exec \
  -H unix:///tmp/moby.sock --iptables=false &

Third, point any standard Docker CLI at that socket, pull something AI-flavored, and run it. The moby tree builds the daemon, not the client, so use the CLI you already have:

export DOCKER_HOST=unix:///tmp/moby.sock
docker version
docker pull pytorch/pytorch
docker run --rm pytorch/pytorch \
  python -c "import torch; print(torch.__version__)"

That docker run exercises the whole tour in one shot: the client POSTs to the create and start routes, the daemon mounts a rootfs view, attaches a network sandbox, launches the task, and streams the Python output back. On a Linux host with an NVIDIA driver, the engine’s device plumbing in daemon/devices_nvidia_linux.go is what makes GPU requests possible, which is precisely how inference images get access to accelerators. Note that the snapshotter-based image store requires a running containerd; if the supervisor cannot start, the daemon falls back to the graphdriver store and the diagrams above suddenly become very concrete.

Honest Limits

This is a static source read, not a runtime study. We did not benchmark startup latency, memory overhead, or pull throughput, and we make no performance claims. The tour reflects master as of this writing — the codebase moves quickly, and the recent absorption of the HTTP server into daemon/server means older blog posts and books point at paths that no longer exist. We covered Linux-centric paths; Windows isolation, Swarm-mode internals under daemon/cluster.go and the swarm router, the BuildKit builder integration, and the plugin system each deserve their own tour. Finally, the diagrams are hand-curated views of a much larger graph — the sparse checkout we analyzed spans well over ten thousand Go files — so treat them as a reading order, not an exhaustive map. If you spot drift between this post and the tree, trust the code and the linked line numbers.
entry.summary: A guided walk through the Docker Engine's Go source, from the dockerd entrypoint through the HTTP API, container start-up, and the graphdriver versus snapshotter storage split.

entry.title: Inside runc: A Source Tour of the OCI Runtime That Boots Every AI Container

link.title: Inside runc: A Source Tour of the OCI Runtime That Boots Every AI Container

entry.content:
Every GPU inference workload you have ever run bottoms out in the same few thousand lines of Go. Whether a vLLM server is scheduled by Kubernetes, pulled by CRI-O, launched through containerd, or started by the Docker engine, the final hop is identical: some higher-level system hands a bundle to runc, and runc asks the Linux kernel for a handful of namespaces, a cgroup, and a fresh root filesystem. All the AI-specific magic above — model registries, schedulers, device plugins — eventually collapses into two syscalls a Python engineer never thinks about: clone(2) and unshare(2). If you want to understand why a pod gets a private network, a memory ceiling, and its own /proc, there is no better Go codebase to read than this one.

runc is the reference implementation of the OCI runtime specification, and its README describes it plainly: “a CLI tool for spawning and running containers on Linux according to the OCI specification.” It has no daemon, no image store, no REST API. Its two-phase lifecycle is what container engines build on: runc create freezes the container’s boundaries while its init process waits, and runc start lets the user’s process run. In this post we walk that path through the actual source on the main branch, from a CLI flag all the way down to the C bootstrap that joins namespaces.

One finding up front, because it surprised us: the cgroups code you may remember from older tutorials no longer lives inside this repository. On main, the cgroup managers come from a separate opencontainers/cgroups module that runc vendors in.
