The core flow we map below — spec conversion, factory, parent process, re-exec’d runc init, rootfs mounting — is all still here, and the two diagrams in this post reflect this exact snapshot of the tree.

The overview: two runc processes cooperate on every container. The parent CLI loads an OCI bundle, builds a Container through the factory, then forks a re-exec'd "runc init" child that joins the namespaces and builds the rootfs.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • main, L88 builds the CLI app and registers createCommand, runCommand, startCommand and friends at L141, defaulting the state root to /run/runc at L98.
  • createCommand, L11 is thin: its Action calls startContainer(cmd, CT_ACT_CREATE, nil) at L67, and runCommand, L12 does the same with CT_ACT_RUN at L81.
  • startContainer, L381 reads config.json via setupSpec (L385), calls createContainer, L184 at L400, then hands the container to runner.run, L223 at L431.
  • createContainer, L184 converts the spec with CreateLibcontainerConfig, L384 at L189 and finishes with libcontainer.Create at L203.
  • Create, L35 validates the container ID, securejoins the state directory under the root (L48), builds a cgroup manager via manager.New at L58, and returns a *Container built at L94.
  • runner.run, L223 dispatches on the action: container.Start for create at L290 and container.Run for run at L294 — both funnel into Container.start, L318.
  • newParentProcess, L496 re-execs the binary itself as runc init at L530, passing _LIBCONTAINER_INITPIPE and _LIBCONTAINER_SYNCPIPE file descriptors (L554-L560).
  • initProcess.start, L789 on the parent side runs cmd.Start (L791), applies cgroups with manager.Apply at L837 — deliberately before the child can fork anything — and streams the bootstrap data at L859.
  • On the child side, Init, L106 enters startInitialization, L128, which dispatches through containerInit, L241 to the standard or setns init implementation.

The detail view: specconv's four converters, the factory and its cgroup manager, the parent-side initProcess, the C-level nsexec bootstrap, and the child-side rootfs assembly, with the setns path for runc exec on the side.

The Bundle: config.json Plus a Rootfs

runc never sees an image. It consumes an OCI bundle: a directory containing one config.json and one populated rootfs/ directory. The create command’s own documentation states this exactly (create.go, L19-L21). The runc spec subcommand can generate a starter config.json for you — spec.go writes it at L116 with mode 0666 — and its help text even shows the classic sed trick to change the default args (L43).

Everything else is translation work. The spec’s linux section — namespaces, uid/gid mappings, resources, seccomp, masked and readonly paths — must become libcontainer’s internal configs.Config. That happens in CreateLibcontainerConfig, L384, with three helpers worth naming: CreateCgroupConfig, L772 converts linux.resources into cgroup rules, setupUserNamespace, L1074 applies uid/gid maps, and SetupSeccomp, L1188 shapes the syscall filter. If you want to know why your GPU pod’s memory limit landed in one cgroup file and not another, this file is where the decision was made. The factory also runs the finished config through a validator — validate.Validate is invoked at Create, L42 — so impossible combinations are rejected before any process is forked.

Create: From a Flag to clone(2)

The clever part of runc’s design is that the “container” is created twice: once as a data structure in the parent, once as a process inside new namespaces. The parent-side Container is just a struct (container_linux.go, L33) holding the config, the state directory, and the cgroup manager. Nothing has forked yet.

When Container.start, L318 runs, it first creates the exec fifo that runc start will later use as a gate (L333), then builds the parent process. newParentProcess, L496 makes a safe copy of the runc binary and re-execs it with the init argument — see the exec.Command(exePath, "init") at L530. The comments around L502 explain the threat model: a container must never be able to tamper with the very binary that is about to jail it. Just above, at L350-L356, you can also read how the fix for CVE-2024-21626 works: every non-stdio file descriptor is marked close-on-exec before runc init is spawned. The sealing itself is delegated to exeseal.CloneSelfExe at L521, which tries an overlayfs-sealed copy first and falls back to a plain temporary copy.

Namespace configuration travels to the child as data, not as flags. newInitProcess, L625 packs the result of Namespaces.CloneFlags, L24 — the mapping of NEWNET, NEWNS, NEWPID and friends onto the kernel’s CLONE_* bits at L12-L17 — into a netlink message via bootstrapData, L1043. The child does not even reach the Go runtime before namespaces are handled: nsenter.go runs nsexec() at L14 as a C constructor, and nsexec.c clones the final child at L322, then setnses into each namespace fd at L560 or unshares a user namespace at L675.

Namespaces, Cgroups, and the Rootfs Illusion

After the child exists, the parent finishes its half in initProcess.start, L789: cgroups are applied first (L837) so no process can escape the limit window, and the deferred block at L805-L820 even converts an OOM kill into a human-readable error.

The child’s half is linuxStandardInit.Init, L51, and it reads like a checklist of what “a container” means. Network interfaces and routes are configured (L81, L84). Then prepareRootfs, L170 makes the root real: prepareRoot, L1100 makes the rootfs mount private, each OCI mount is applied by setupAndMountToRootfs, L114 (with mountToRootfs, L606 dispatching per target type), and finally the process is jailed — pivot_root at L1152, with chroot at L1266 and msMoveRoot at L1203 as fallbacks. finalizeRootfs, L281 remounts deferred read-only mounts so a “readonly rootfs” really is one. The tail of Init applies SELinux and AppArmor profiles — L139 — plus sysctls, masked paths, and rlimits (setupRlimits, L615) after finalizeNamespace, L300 drops the setup capabilities.

The second entry path is runc exec. Exec, L217 produces a setns process instead: newSetnsProcess, L654 passes the saved namespace paths, setnsProcess.start, L473 joins the running container, optionally pushing itself into a sub-cgroup at L370, and linuxSetnsInit.Init, L35 finishes on the child side.

From Install to Your First Model

Building runc is the most honest way to demystify it. Per the README, runc only supports Linux; on a Debian-family box install the toolchain with the documented one-liner — apt update && apt install -y make gcc linux-libc-dev libseccomp-dev pkg-config git (L37) — then clone and build:

git clone https://github.com/opencontainers/runc
cd runc
make
sudo make install

That sequence is verbatim from the README (L107-L115), and it leaves the binary at /usr/local/sbin/runc (L126). Confirm what you built with runc --version; the README notes you can append your own suffix via the EXTRA_VERSION make variable (L134), which is handy when you are comparing a patched build against a distro package. Now build the smallest bundle and run it:

mkdir bundle && cd bundle && mkdir rootfs
runc spec                       # writes config.json
runc run hello                  # or: runc create hello && runc start hello

For a first model, unpack any inference-runtime image’s layer tarball into bundle/rootfs, point config.json at the server binary, and run the same two commands — the kernel-side machinery you just read about is the entire difference between “a process” and “an inference container”. Rootless works too: createContainer passes RootlessEUID: os.Geteuid() != 0 (utils_linux.go, L195), specconv then adds user namespace mappings, and the log warning at process_linux.go, L841-L846 tells you exactly which rootless-cgroup corner you are in.

Where runc Sits in the Stack

The diagrams above explain a lot of upstream behavior for free. containerd’s task layer and its per-container shims ultimately shell out to exactly the create/start pair described in our containerd source tour. The Docker engine reaches the same code through containerd, as covered in the moby deep dive. CRI-O calls runc most directly of all, since the Kubernetes CRI expects a low-level runtime — see the CRI-O walkthrough — and kubelet’s scheduling decisions only ever become real when the Kubernetes control plane lands a pod that some runtime turns into an initProcess.start call. Same clone, same cgroup, same pivot_root, every time.

Honest Limits

This tour sticks to claims the source itself supports. runc is Linux-only (README, L26); there is no Windows or macOS story here. It manages no images and no networks beyond the namespace plumbing shown above — a bundle’s rootfs/ must already be populated, and the repo contains no pull or layer-apply code on this path. The cgroup managers it uses come from the separate opencontainers/cgroups module referenced at factory_linux.go, L58, so line-level behavior of cgroup v1 versus v2 lives outside this repository. All line numbers cite the main branch as of this snapshot (commit 130fae39f3c7); runc moves fast, and code comments — like the CVE-2024-21626 hardening note — are the first things that change. We ran no benchmarks and make no performance claims; the value of reading this source is architectural, not quantitative.
entry.summary: A line-by-line tour of the opencontainers/runc source showing how create and start really work: namespaces, clone, cgroups, and rootfs setup.

entry.title: Apache APISIX Under the Hood: The etcd-Driven Gateway Built for AI Traffic

link.title: Apache APISIX Under the Hood: The etcd-Driven Gateway Built for AI Traffic

entry.content:
Every serious AI stack hits the same wall eventually: model servers, vector databases, and agent backends all grow from a handful of services into a zoo of endpoints, each with its own auth scheme, its own rate limits, and its own idea of what a “normal” request looks like. Something has to sit in front of that zoo and make it presentable — terminating TLS, checking API keys, smoothing bursty traffic, and steering a /v1/chat/completions call to the right pool of GPUs. That something is an API gateway, and for inference-heavy workloads the gateway is not plumbing; it is the control surface for your entire serving budget.

Apache APISIX is an Apache Software Foundation gateway built on top of NGINX and etcd — its README says exactly that — with dynamic routing and hot-reloading of plugins as the headline features. It is written in Lua and runs inside OpenResty, the NGINX-plus-LuaJIT runtime, which means every request is handled by Lua functions woven directly into NGINX’s own request phases. Config is not baked into a config file at deploy time: the gateway watches etcd continuously, and route changes take effect within moments of an API call, with no reload and no dropped connections. Where Kong shares the same OpenResty foundation but traditionally keeps its source of truth in PostgreSQL, APISIX makes etcd the single source of truth and treats the data plane as a pure projection of it. If you read the earlier Traefik tour, you will notice the opposite philosophy again — Traefik is Go-native and provider-driven, while APISIX is C-adjacent, Lua-native, and store-driven.

The best way to understand a gateway like this is to trace one request through the source. This post walks the master branch of apache/apisix: how the worker boots, how routes are matched, how plugins are loaded and ordered, how upstreams are balanced, and where the Admin API fits in. Two diagrams anchor the tour — an overview first, then a deeper map — and every symbol referenced below was checked directly against the repository before being cited.

The APISIX surface at a glance: one CLI command boots OpenResty workers; the config store (etcd, or a local YAML file in standalone mode) feeds routes to the router; every request passes the access phase, the plugin framework, and the load balancer before reaching your upstream; the Admin API writes config back to etcd.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • CLI entry — start(), L1087 in the CLI turns apisix start into a rendered nginx.conf and a running OpenResty instance; the same module documents the stop and restart verbs around L178.
  • Worker bootstrap — http_init_worker(), L120 seeds randomness, starts the event bus, the LRU cache, timers, and then wires the config watcher, plugin framework, router, and Admin API handlers into the worker, one require(...).init_worker() per line through L172.
  • Config store — sync_data(), L722 in the etcd config module polls and watches etcd prefixes, while its counterpart sync_data(), L245 serves the same role for standalone-mode YAML files; which one is active is decided by core.lua, L34.
  • Router — router.lua, L81 builds the configured HTTP router; the default radixtree_uri match, L30 resolves one route per request using a radixtree keyed by URI, host, and vars.
  • Access phase — http_access_phase(), L915 is the per-request workhorse: it fetches a pooled api_ctx, matches the route, merges service and consumer configuration, and hands plugins their turn.
  • Plugin framework — plugin.load(), L420 requires every enabled plugin module once per worker; run_plugin(), L1362 then executes each plugin’s phase hook in priority order on every request.
  • Upstream and balancer — set_by_route(), L381 normalizes nodes, scheme, and TLS, after which pick_server(), L275 chooses a healthy node through the balancer module named by upstream.type (L154).
  • Admin API — run(), L176 dispatches REST calls on port 9180 to resource handlers like admin/routes.lua, L183, guarded by check_token(), L80.

The detailed map: request phases and the router on top, the plugin framework and a sample of built-in plugins in the middle, balancers and config providers below, with the Admin API closing the loop back into etcd.

From Install to Your First Model

The quickstart from the README is one command: curl -sL https://run.api7.ai/apisix/quickstart | sh. That script brings up APISIX listening on port 9080 together with its etcd configuration store. Confirm it is alive the README way: curl "http://127.0.0.1:9080" --head | grep Server — and watch for APISIX in the server header.

The first route is an Admin API call against port 9180:

curl -i "http://127.0.0.1:9180/apisix/admin/routes/1" -X PUT -d '
{
  "uri": "/get",
  "upstream": {
    "type": "roundrobin",
    "nodes": {
      "httpbin.org:80": 1
    }
  }
}'

A moment later, curl "http://127.0.0.1:9080/get" returns the httpbin response — the gateway proxied your first request without any reload. What happened under the hood is the part worth savoring: the Admin API validated the route schema in check_conf(), L54, wrote it into etcd, the etcd watcher picked up the change, and the router rebuilt its radixtree in each worker. None of that touched a config file.

From here the jump to model serving is exactly one more plugin. APISIX now advertises itself as an AI gateway, and the README lists the pieces: AI proxying to different LLM providers through a unified interface, load balancing with retries and fallbacks across multiple LLMs, token-based rate limiting to control cost, and security for AI workloads. In the source, that is the ai-* plugin family — ai-proxy, L56 rewrites a request into a provider’s API shape during the access phase and delegates to a provider module selected by conf.provider (L40), while ai-rate-limiting, L295 enforces token windows in the same phase. Because these are ordinary plugins with ordinary priorities, the same gateway that protects your /get demo also fronts your inference fleet, and pairing it with a Python backend built on FastAPI keeps the auth and throttling story in one place.

The Config Model: Watches, Not Reloads

The most distinctive design decision in APISIX is that nothing configures NGINX at request time — everything configures etcd, and the data plane follows. The etcd cluster holds every route, service, upstream, consumer, and plugin config as versioned keys. Each worker process runs a watcher for the prefixes it cares about: config_etcd.lua allocates a store per key with new(), L1053, starts its timers in init_worker(), L1256, and then loops in sync_data() fetching changed keys and firing an event per update. Consumers of a resource — the router, the plugin loader, the balancer — recompute their in-memory structures from those events.

This is why route changes propagate without downtime, and it is a genuinely different trade from gateways that re-render a config file and ask NGINX to reload. It is also why the standalone mode exists: config_yaml.lua implements the same resource interface on top of a local apisix.yaml file, polling its mtime in _automatic_fetch(), L421. The README calls this out as the friendly option under Kubernetes, where etcd’s operational overhead is a cost you did not ask for. The selection logic is a two-liner in core.lua, L24: read deployment.config_provider from the local conf, default to etcd, and require apisix.core.config_ plus that name.

One subtlety deserves emphasis: the Admin API and the data plane are peers, not master and minion. check_token() compares the X-API-Key header (or query argument or cookie) against the admin_key configured under deployment.admin; if you disable that check, you are trusting your network. The Admin API is served by the same OpenResty workers — http_admin() is just another phase hook — which keeps the deployment story to one binary plus one store.

Plugins: Lua Functions With a Priority Number

A plugin in APISIX is a Lua module that declares a name, a version, a priority, a JSON schema for its config, and hooks named after NGINX phases: rewrite, access, header_filter, body_filter, log. The framework sorts every plugin list by descending priority in sort_plugin(), L142 — higher numbers run first — and then calls only the hooks a phase needs. The numbers are a real routing decision: key-auth at priority 2500 runs its consumer lookup in rewrite, L110 before anything downstream sees the request; proxy-rewrite at 1008 mutates the upstream URI and headers in rewrite, L309; limit-req at 1001 shape-checks request rate in access, L138; prometheus at 500 collects metrics from its own api(), L105 endpoint instead of the request path.

The per-request glue is plugin.filter(), L575: given the matched route, it assembles the plugin list from route config, service config, and the authenticated consumer, so a single request can stack plugin configs from three levels. Merging happens before filtering — merge_service_route(), L763 folds service-level plugins into the route — and once a consumer is authenticated, consumer-level config can add plugins mid-request and even rerun the rewrite stage for the newcomers, which you can see at the bottom of the access phase around L1071.

The plugins directory holds well over a hundred modules, from jwt-auth to kafka-logger to the ai-* family, and the enabled list is itself config: plugin.load() reads it from the local conf at L421. In practice you enable a dozen, disable the rest, and pay only for the hooks you use — an execution model that keeps the Lua-per-request cost predictable.

Balancing Real Traffic

When the access phase finishes, handle_upstream() resolves the upstream: either an inline upstream object on the route, an upstream_id reference (including one chosen at runtime by the traffic-split plugin), or a domain that needs DNS resolution — see handle_upstream(), L716. set_by_route(), L381 then normalizes nodes into host-port-weight tuples, resolves scheme and TLS options, and fills in per-node details.

Node selection lives in pick_server(), L275. It consults active health checks, filters out unhealthy and warming-up nodes, and delegates to a picker module loaded dynamically by upstream type at L154: weighted round-robin in balancer/roundrobin.lua, L27, least-connections in balancer/least_conn.lua, L115, plus consistent hashing, EWMA, and priority-based pickers. After NGINX proxies the request, the balancer phase at http_balancer_phase(), L1662 can pick a different node on retry — for inference traffic, where one backend occasionally times out mid-generation, that retry path is the difference between a 502 page and a slow-but-successful answer.

Honest Limits

  • Two stores to operate. etcd is the heartbeat of APISIX, and it is a distributed system in its own right — quorum tuning, compaction, and backups are now part of your on-call rotation. Standalone YAML mode removes etcd but also removes hot config from remote sources.
  • Lua all the way down. The plugin model is a gift if you can write Lua, a chore if you cannot. WASM and external-plugin escapes exist, but the mainstream path is Lua on LuaJIT, and debugging a priority clash between twenty plugins is a skill you will build the hard way.
  • The Admin API is a control plane on the same box. Port 9180 is guarded by a single static API key from config, and it lives inside the same workers as the data plane. Front it with TLS and network policy, or it becomes the most interesting endpoint on the host.
  • Benchmarks are yours to run. The README makes no performance claims, and neither should you copy anyone else’s. The one number that matters is measured against your routes, your plugins, and your model servers.
  • The project moves fast. This tour reflects master at the time of writing; anchors can drift as the code evolves, which is exactly why every link in this post points at a pinned commit path you can re-check.

The verdict, in one line: if your traffic is API-shaped, bursty, and increasingly AI-shaped, APISIX is the rare gateway whose architecture — store-driven config, phase-native plugins, health-aware balancing — matches the problem rather than merely covering it. The source is approachable once you see the seams, and the two diagrams above are the map to keep open while you read it.

entry.title: Caddy: The Go Web Server Where HTTPS Is Not Your Job

link.title: Caddy: The Go Web Server Where HTTPS Is Not Your Job

entry.content:
Anyone who has put a machine learning model online knows the drill: you wrap a FastAPI app around your inference code, run it on port 8000, and then discover that the real work starts. Getting traffic to it over the public internet means a TLS certificate, a renewal process, an HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect, trusted proxy headers, and a reverse proxy config that quietly becomes the most fragile file you own. The same applies to Grafana dashboards, MinIO object storage, or any UI you bolt onto your ML stack. TLS termination is not glamorous, but it is the front door of every production AI system — and it is exactly the front door where misconfigurations turn into outages or leaks. We compared an alternative edge proxy in our Traefik deep dive, and Caddy takes a strikingly different stance on how that front door should behave.

Caddy is a web server written in Go whose headline feature is printed right at the top of its README: “Every site on HTTPS.” It was the first web server to use HTTPS automatically and by default, obtaining and renewing certificates from ACME authorities like Let’s Encrypt and ZeroSSL with zero configuration, and it manages a local certificate authority for internal names. Under the hood it is better described as an extensible server platform: a small config core plus “apps” (the tls and http apps ship standard), where every app, listener wrapper, matcher, and handler is a module. You can drive it with a friendly Caddyfile, with its native JSON config, or through a REST admin API — and all three converge on the same document.

This post walks through the source of caddyserver/caddy on the master branch with two diagrams and verified line anchors, so you can jump from picture to code. We will follow the life of a config from caddy run to a live listener, trace a request through matchers and the handler chain, and look closely at how automatic HTTPS is wired — including what Caddy does and does not promise.

Overview of Caddy's architecture: the CLI loads and adapts a config, the config core provisions apps, and the HTTP and TLS apps run listeners, routes, and certificate automation side by side.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • cmd.Main, L66 — the CLI entry point that parses OS arguments and dispatches the requested command, including caddy run defined in commands.go, L122.
  • cmdRun, L189 — the run command implementation: it sets resource limits, loads the config through LoadConfig, L107, then blocks while Caddy serves.
  • Adapter.Adapt, L32 — the Caddyfile adapter that lexes and parses your config text into Caddy’s native JSON document.
  • caddy.Load, L115 — the config runtime entry that applies JSON through changeConfig, skipping reloads when nothing actually changed.
  • App.Start, L481 — the HTTP app’s startup, which builds one http.Server per site block and binds every listener address.
  • Server.ServeHTTP, L598 — the per-request entry inside the http app: timeouts, access logging, HTTP/3 advertisement, and ACME challenge handling all happen here before user routes run.
  • RouteList.Compile, L239 — compiles the list of routes, each carrying a match and a handle list, into a single middleware stack.
  • Handler.ServeHTTP, L627 — the reverse_proxy handler, complete with a retry loop over upstream backends.
  • TLS.Start, L406 — the TLS app kicking off certificate management for all “automate” names, backed by the certmagic library that is pinned as a dependency in go.mod, L13.

The overview shows the county lines; the detail map below goes street by street, from the admin API’s localhost:2019 endpoint down to the matcher evaluation inside each route.

Detailed view: the CLI and Caddyfile adapter feed the config core; the admin API mutates the same config; the HTTP app binds listeners and runs the routing chain; the TLS app provisions certmagic policies and answers ACME challenges.

From Install to Your First Site

Caddy’s README is refreshingly blunt about installation: the simplest cross-platform path is to download a binary from GitHub Releases and place the executable in your PATH. If you want to build from source, you need Go 1.26.0 or newer, clone the repo, and build inside cmd/caddy; for plugins or version-stamped binaries there is xcaddy build. There is no runtime dependency chain — the README points out that Caddy runs anywhere with no external dependencies, not even libc.

The fastest possible serving session does not even need a config file. The file-server command is registered in fileserver/command.go, L40 with flags like --root, --listen, and --browse:

caddy file-server --listen :8080

That single line spins up a production-ready static file server on port 8080 — the same FileServer type used inside full configs, whose ServeHTTP lives at staticfiles.go, L329. For a long-running site you would write a Caddyfile instead. A minimal reverse proxy setup that forwards API traffic to a local model server looks like this:

example.com {
    reverse_proxy localhost:8000
}

Run it with caddy run --config Caddyfile. Two interesting things happen: first, cmdRun, L189 calls LoadConfig, which detects the Caddyfile and runs it through Adapter.Adapt, L32; if you are curious what JSON your Caddyfile produces, caddy adapt --config Caddyfile --pretty prints it (the command is defined in commands.go, L281). Second, caddy.Load, L115 applies that JSON, which cascades through changeConfig into run, L419: a context is provisioned, the admin endpoint is swapped in via replaceLocalAdminServer, L376, and every app’s Start is invoked in a loop with rollback if one fails (caddy.go, L444).

While serving, the same config document stays live. The admin API listens on localhost:2019 by default — the constant DefaultAdminListen is defined at admin.go, L1456 — and can POST a new JSON config or PATCH a fragment of it, with requests dispatched through unsyncedConfigAccess, L1181. This is why Caddy reloads never fork a new process: the config is data, swapped in place while listeners stay open.

Automatic HTTPS: certmagic Under the Hood

Automatic HTTPS is not a bolt-on module; it is a separate app that runs alongside the HTTP app. When the TLS app provisions (TLS.Provision, L166), it builds a certmagic certificate cache with a default capacity of 10,000 certificates. When it starts (TLS.Start, L406), it calls t.Manage on every name listed under tls automate, and certmagic — a separate library from the same author, pinned at v0.25.6 in go.mod — takes over issuance and renewal.

The automation rules themselves are declarative. AutomationConfig, L37 and AutomationPolicy, L91 describe which subjects get which issuers, and makeCertMagicConfig, L272 translates a policy into a certmagic config. By default Caddy uses ACME with both ZeroSSL and Let’s Encrypt as issuers (DefaultIssuers, L480), with multi-issuer fallback listed among README features, plus a fully-managed local CA for internal names like localhost.

One detail worth appreciating as a safety design: the HTTP-01 challenge has priority over your routes. Server.ServeHTTP, L598 guarantees ACME HTTP challenges by calling HandleHTTPChallenge, L810 before any user-defined handler chain runs — a stray route can never accidentally shadow your certificate renewals. This is the kind of guardrail you would otherwise have to remember to configure yourself with a hand-rolled proxy setup, and it is a large part of why serving a FastAPI inference app through our FastAPI tutorials behind Caddy “just works” on the TLS side.

The Request Path: Matchers, Routes, Handlers

Once a request arrives, the journey is deliberately boring — in the good sense. Server.serveHTTP, L847 performs hygiene first: it rejects over-long methods, enforces RFC 9112’s Host header requirements, and strips underscore/dot header aliases that could enable spoofing. Then the compiled primary chain runs at L950, wrapped by enforcementHandler, L963.

Routes are the heart of the http app. Each Route, L31 carries matcher sets under the JSON key match and handlers under handle; matcher sets are OR’ed while matchers inside a set are AND’ed. At request time wrapRoute, L256 evaluates the matchers — MatchHost.Match, L304 even uses a binary search fast path for large host lists — and, on a match, executes the route’s handler chain in middleware order. Handlers that produce a response (like file_server or reverse_proxy) belong at the end of a route, because the request flows down the chain and the response flows back up.

The reverse proxy handler deserves its own paragraph for the AI-serving use case. The Handler struct at L107 carries upstream pools, load balancing, health checks, transports, and a flush_interval that defaults to immediate flushing for streaming responses — exactly what you want when a language model is emitting tokens. proxyLoopIteration, L749 selects an upstream per attempt and drives retries, while roundTrip, L1639 performs the actual upstream round trip. If you deploy models on Kubernetes, this is the machinery answering your Service endpoints.

Running Caddy for Inference Endpoints

For an ML stack, a realistic Caddyfile fronts several services at once: an inference API, a dashboard, and maybe static model artifacts. Because routes are matcher-based, host and path dispatch live in one document, and the admin API means you can add a route with a curl call instead of restarting. Prometheus-style metrics scraping of your services also flows through the same listeners — see our Prometheus setup notes for the collector side.

Operations-wise, caddy start (defined at commandfuncs.go, L46 as cmdStart) launches Caddy in the background by spawning a child run process with a pingback confirmation handshake, so failed startups surface as errors instead of silent background deaths. Config survives restarts through an autosave file, and caddy reload swaps a new config into a running process over the admin API.

Honest Limits

Caddy’s automatic HTTPS depends on public reachability: ACME issuance requires that your domain resolves and that ports 80/443 are reachable, so it will not help inside air-gapped clusters — there you use the internal CA and accept untrusted roots, or bring your own certificates via certificate loaders. The code is also honest about on-demand TLS risk: TLS.Start, L406 logs a warning — “YOUR SERVER MAY BE VULNERABLE TO ABUSE” — when on-demand issuance is enabled without an ask endpoint or permission module, because otherwise any hostname hitting your server triggers a certificate request.

The Caddyfile, while delightful, is a projection of the JSON config, and README is explicit that JSON is the native language; some advanced configurations are only reachable in JSON, and adapters exist precisely because the Caddyfile cannot express everything. Placement of handlers also matters — the route compilation makes handler ordering meaningful, which is a learning curve if you come from an nginx-style include model. Finally, the trademark README insists the software is called “Caddy”, not “Caddy Server”, and the default admin endpoint binds to localhost:2019 only; exposing it to a network is a deliberate, opt-in decision you should make with an auth policy in mind. None of these are disqualifying — they are the edges of a design that leans hard on sensible defaults, and knowing the edges is what makes the defaults trustworthy.
